extracted.intended_audience: communication researchers, journalism educators, and journalism scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the cognitive criteria journalists use during the newswriting process, emphasizing reliance on discourse conventions vs. direct audience knowledge. Based on protocol (think-aloud) recordings of science journalists composing articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourse Knowledge (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An array of rhetorical choices about 'appropriate formats, matters of tone, diction, stance toward the reader, kinds of allowable openings, structure, evidence, and argument' (Park, 1986).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourse knowledge is information about standards and conventions of a particular genre of writing that writers call into working memory to make decisions. It can be tacit but may surface in consciousness and exert a direct, powerful influence on composing. Writers use discourse knowledge to make sense of what they are writing and to ensure conformity with accepted standards of the journalistic community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourse Community / Sources of Discourse Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers obtain discourse knowledge from belonging to a 'discourse community' — a group bound by common interest that communicates through approved channels and regulates discourse (Porter, 1986).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourse knowledge is learned by reading texts published in approved forums and through educational training, professional experience, interactions with colleagues, handing texts to colleagues for feedback, revising guided by editors, and modeling prior texts. These practices teach accepted topics, organizational structures, styles, and 'what works' in the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Knowledge (contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about audience members' knowledge, needs, interests, experiences, beliefs, attitudes, and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although traditional advice tells journalists to 'write for the readers,' the study found journalists rarely recalled audience knowledge into working memory while composing. Examples show few references to audience needs; when present, they were often idiosyncratic ('if it's interesting to me it's probably interesting to other people'). This criterion functions more as an expected orientation than an active decision guide for the observed writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: News Values
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional news values such as prominence, timeliness, proximity, rarity and consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These values provide the cognitive basis for decisions about selection, attention, understanding, representation and uses of news. In this study news values had the least direct impact during the writing phase (more influential during story selection), though examples show timeliness affecting choice of topics (e.g., war-related interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear writing achieved through precise word choice, concise and direct sentence structure, grammatically-correct sentences, logical progression of thought between paragraphs, logical text organization, and sufficient background information and explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists actively monitor and revise for clarity during composing: marking passages as 'too colloquial,' substituting words ('Not rather, but more likely'), removing redundancy ('This is redundant, redundant material'), reorganizing paragraphs ('Move that quote paragraph up'), and ensuring appropriate level of explanation for readers. Concern about repetition and organization frequently guided editing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: The creation of images or pictures and appealing to the senses through rich description, colorful language and literary techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers assess and try to improve vividness to 'grab' readers (selecting a 'grabby' lead, inserting images). Vividness can be consciously traded off against other criteria (example: 'Lose a little bit of credibility... Makes it a bit punchier'). Some journalists deliberately choose punchier phrasing or images to increase interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing that is accurate, factual and impartial; includes use of quotations and careful sourcing to enhance trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists use quotes to 'achieve distance' and to back claims, are meticulous about quoting sources verbatim, check wording and timing of quotes, verify facts, check spelling and titles, and evaluate sources' expertise. Practices include keeping files of quotes, planning where to place quotes in a story, and calling authoritative institutions to corroborate information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production Constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical limits on space and time that affect composing (e.g., required length, deadlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists 'write to space' and work under deadline pressure; they monitor word counts/lines ('Word count 386...'), limit or cut material based on length, and are affected by time constraints (checking the clock). Severity of constraints determines how strongly this criterion shapes decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional Register / Mode of Address / Public Idiom
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper's or community's conventional register — an accepted, imposed, or expected way of writing — sometimes described as the 'public idiom' or 'mode of address.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists learn to address audiences by modeling the discourse community's public idiom; the newspaper's version of public language forms the basis for reciprocity between producer and reader. Conventional register influences choices of tone, diction and rhetorical strategies, and often governs decisions more than specific audience knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational Structure (as a distinct compositional concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangement of material within an article: paragraph breaks, ordering of general vs. specific information, placement of examples and quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists actively reorganize material while composing to improve clarity and flow ('Start a new graph here,' 'Maybe I should just move this discovery... into the second paragraph'). Organizational decisions are driven by discourse conventions about how stories should be structured for readability and explanation.
